# Porcelain Ingestion and Cylinder Damage in EcoBoost Engines

When a spark plug porcelain fragment breaks off and falls into a combustion chamber, it is no longer a simple ignition issue; it becomes an internal mechanical hazard. In your 2016 Ford Mustang EcoBoost scenario, the situation escalated quickly once that chunk of ceramic entered the cylinder. While swapping all four plugs is standard preventative maintenance for these engines to ensure consistent firing order and voltage distribution, losing a piece of the insulator during removal changes the failure mode entirely.

The immediate danger lies in what happens when the engine cranks with debris inside. The porcelain fragment likely lodged itself on a valve or, more critically, impinged upon the cylinder wall or piston skirt. When you started the engine briefly to attempt blowing the pieces out via the exhaust, you confirmed that not all material was expelled. This partial removal left enough residue to cause intermittent contact between the moving parts and the debris.

Modern EcoBoost engines operate at high RPMs with tight tolerances designed for performance, not durability against internal abrasion. A single shard of hard ceramic acting as an abrasive can score the cylinder wall or gouge the piston ring land. This scoring disrupts the compression seal, leading to the exact symptoms you are describing: intermittent misfires that vary by day and load. On days when the debris hasn't caught on a valve, the engine runs fine. When it does catch, the air-fuel mixture is disrupted, or the compression drops momentarily, causing sputtering.

### Why the "Blow Out" Method Failed

The tactic of starting the engine to blow out debris relies on air pressure forcing foreign objects through the exhaust system. This works only if the object is loose and small enough to pass the intake and cylinder volume without snagging. In your case, the shop removed "most but not all" pieces. The remaining fragments are likely wedged in a way that prevents them from being expelled by airflow alone.

Once debris embeds itself or creates a scoring pattern on the metal surfaces, vibration and heat can work it further into crevices. This makes retrieval increasingly difficult without disassembling the cylinder head. Attempting to run the engine now risks converting a localized issue into catastrophic damage, such as a cracked piston or bent valve, which would require an engine rebuild or replacement.

### Diagnostic Path Forward

Since you have already replaced the ignition coil and are experiencing persistent rough running, continuing to swap components like plugs will yield no results because the root cause is mechanical, not electrical. The next logical step requires a visual inspection of the internal combustion environment.

A borescope inspection is necessary before committing to further parts or scrapping the vehicle. A mechanic can insert a flexible camera through the spark plug tube hole to view the condition of the piston crown and cylinder walls for scoring marks. If significant damage is visible, the cost of repairing the engine may exceed the value of the car, validating the other mechanic's suggestion to sell. However, if the score marks are light and localized, cleaning the area or running a short-time break-in procedure with specific additives might mitigate the issue temporarily.

There is no software command or diagnostic code that can clear physical debris from a cylinder. The decision matrix here is strict: inspect internally first. If the engine is deemed salvageable, proceed with caution. If the damage extends to the piston rings or head gasket sealing surfaces, the cost of repair often outweighs the remaining equity in a 2016 Mustang EcoBoost.

For developers and engineers who treat software systems like mechanical ones: sometimes the error isn't in the logic (the coil), but in the runtime environment (the cylinder). When hardware fails physically, no amount of code refactoring or configuration tuning can restore performance without replacing the compromised component.
